title: The Best Manager in the Company Has to Be You
author: Managing The Future
summary: Managing The Future argues that at scale, organizational quality is a function of managerial quality -- and that a CEO or founder who accepts a management team that is merely adequate is implicitly accepting a mediocre company. The article challenges the common rationalization that a company can survive a weak management team if the product is strong or the mission is compelling. Drawing on the principle that the quality of a company at scale equals the quality of its management team, the piece argues that every tolerance of managerial underperformance creates a hidden tax on everything the company does. The practical implication: leaders should hold their management team to the same rigor they apply to product decisions, and should actively develop managers with the same intentionality they apply to technical systems.
points: Organizational quality at scale is determined by management quality: the product, mission, and culture can carry a company early, but past a certain size, manager quality defines the ceiling.
Tolerating mediocre management is an implicit strategic choice: every underperforming manager creates a hidden tax on team output, talent retention, and execution quality.
The rationalization that strong product can compensate for weak management breaks down at scale: management quality becomes the binding constraint on growth, coordination, and execution.

Leaders must develop managers with the same intentionality applied to product and systems: management excellence doesn't emerge organically -- it requires investment, feedback, and deliberate practice.
The 'best manager in the company' standard is a frame, not a boast: it asks each leader to aspire to be the benchmark rather than the acceptable floor for managerial practice.
quotes: The quality of a company at scale is equal to the quality of the management team.
Every mediocre manager is a hidden tax. You pay it in missed goals, in talent you didn't keep, in decisions that got made badly or not at all.
The product can carry you for a while. The mission can carry you. But eventually the management team becomes the binding constraint on everything you're trying to build.
If you want a world-class company, you have to insist on world-class management. That starts with you. Not as a standard you impose on others, but as a commitment you make to yourself.
Developing great managers is not a luxury or an HR function. It is the strategic work of leadership.
